partial_case.facts: The resident moved in to the property in November 2023 and she reported damp and mould in her hallway, in January 2024. In March 2024, the landlord identified that the damp was caused by an issue with guttering. The guttering was repaired and between June and August 2024, it stripped back the hallway, replastered and redecorated. However, it failed to ensure the walls were dry, which meant damp and mould returned and the work needed redoing. The complaint was brought to us in May 2025 once all work had been completed, as the resident was unhappy with the level of compensation offered by the landlord. The resident complained the landlord had failed to repair guttering that had been causing damp and mould in her hallway since January 2024. The landlord offered the resident £950 compensation: £700 for the disruption caused and £250 for the inconvenience of not following its complaints policy or procedure. The £950 was paid to the resident on 11 December 2024. The landlord finalised all outstanding works and offered additional compensation to the resident of £800. This was made up of £500 for delays completing all works and disruption to her home (£100 per month since the stage 2 response). It also offered a further £300 compensation to acknowledge the resident having to chase for information. This was paid to the resident on 2 May 2025. The resident referred the complaint to us as she was unhappy with the compensation offered, as the works had taken 15 months.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: While there were issues with the way the landlord handled the repairs needed to address the damp at the property, it acknowledged these failings and took steps to try and put things right by offering a reasonable amount of compensation to the resident.

The landlord acknowledged its failings and the £1,500 compensation offered was in line with its own guidance, as it reflected that overall, the resident suffered "serious disruption". The amount offered is also in line with this Service's Remedies guidance for findings of severe maladministration. As a result, the Ombudsman would have made the same or similar award in the circumstances and we therefore find that the landlord has made an offer which was reasonable and proportionate to resolve the complaint.

claim_types: Handling of reported water ingress, damp and mould
evidence: The Ombudsman considered the landlord’s damp and mould, responsive repairs, complaints, compensation and remedies policies.
The Ombudsman considered the Ombudsman’s own Spotlight on Damp and Mould report and Remedies guidance.
The decision refers to landlord records indicating that no one was actively monitoring the work or ensuring the resident was regularly updated.
The decision refers to evidence that the resident became increasingly frustrated by lack of action and having to chase responses.
partial_case.facts: The resident moved into the property in November 2023 and reported damp and mould in the hallway in January 2024. In March 2024, the landlord identified guttering as the cause of the damp; guttering was repaired and hallway works were carried out between June and August 2024, but the damp and mould returned and works needed redoing. The complaint concerned the landlord’s handling of reported water ingress, damp and mould, and complaint handling. On 4 April 2024, the resident complained that the landlord had failed to repair guttering causing damp and mould since January 2024. The landlord issued a stage 1 response on 21 June 2024 and the resident escalated to stage 2 on 18 July 2024 because repair work to the hallway remained outstanding. The landlord issued its stage 2 response on 29 November 2024, acknowledged failings, apologised, and offered £950 compensation, which was paid on 11 December 2024. On 23 April 2025, the landlord finalised outstanding works and offered additional compensation of £800, which was paid on 2 May 2025. On 16 May 2025, the resident referred the complaint because she was unhappy with the compensation offered and said the works had taken 15 months.
partial_case.ground_truth_outcome: Reasonable redress was offered for both the landlord’s handling of reported water ingress, damp and mould and its handling of the formal complaint; no orders were made.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: While there were issues with the way the landlord handled the repairs needed to address the damp at the property, it acknowledged these failings and took steps to try and put things right by offering a reasonable amount of compensation to the resident.
The landlord did not adhere to its Complaints policy and there were delays addressing the complaint, but it offered compensation that sufficiently recognised the impact this had on the resident.

The landlord acknowledged its failings and the £1,500 compensation offered was in line with its own guidance, as it reflected that overall, the resident suffered “serious disruption”. The amount offered is also in line with this Service’s Remedies guidance for findings of severe maladministration. As a result, the Ombudsman would have made the same or similar award in the circumstances and we therefore find that the landlord has made an offer which was reasonable and proportionate to resolve the complaint.

The landlord’s Compensation and Remedies policy says where there has been a severe failure in its complaint handling, compensation of between £201 and £300 should be considered. There was an extensive failure by the landlord to follow it Complaints policy, which caused a significant impact on the complainant. This was recognised by the landlord when it responded at stage 2 and its offer of £250 compensation is in line not only with its own guidance, but also ours. We have therefore made a finding of reasonable redress on that basis.
